cultivar: Sichuan medium- and small-leaf population bushes of the Ya'an, Mingshan and Yingjing hills
processing: Post-fermented by several cycles of steaming and piling ('zuo se') over days to weeks, dried, then steamed and pressed into bricks of various sizes (Kang Zhuan, the larger Jin Jian, and modern small bricks and cubes) or sold loose.
harvest_season: Summer and autumn pickings of mature leaf and stems for the traditional bricks; the modern consumer line uses somewhat finer spring and summer leaf.
appearance_dry: Dark, firm bricks from 500 g down to bite-sized cubes, or loose coarse brown leaf with stems; the traditional bricks come in yellow paper and bamboo bundles.
taste_profile: Smooth, woody and sweet with a mild earthiness, a faint smoky warmth and a long, rounded finish without bitterness; finer modern lots are cleaner and a little fruitier.

brewing.notes: Simmer 10 g per litre for 5–10 minutes for the traditional cup, or rinse twice and brew with boiling water in a clay pot; small cubes are made for a thermos.

vintage_note: Sold by pressing year and factory, from the traditional 500 g Kang Zhuan and larger Jin Jian bricks to small gift bricks, cubes and loose packs; the modern consumer products are mostly 1–5 years old, traditional bricks 1–10 years, with older bricks traded as collectables.
description:
Ya'an Zang Cha is the modern umbrella name for the dark teas of Ya'an in western Sichuan – 'Tibetan tea', because for most of their history they were made for Tibet and drunk there as butter tea. The name became a protected origin in the 2000s, and under it sit the traditional border bricks (Kang Zhuan and the larger, coarser Jin Jian) and a new line of small bricks, cubes, gift boxes and loose tea aimed at Chinese city drinkers who want the tea without the thirty-kilo bundle.

All of it is made by the Ya'an method of repeated steaming and piling, which the makers describe as 'making colour': fired and rolled leaf is heaped warm and damp, steamed, heaped again, and the cycle repeated until the leaf is evenly dark, before drying and pressing. It is a slower, gentler darkening than the single big pile of ripe pu-erh, and it gives a tea that is smooth and woody rather than earthy or muddy.

In the cup expect wood, a deep sweetness, a mild earthiness and a faint smoky warmth, with a rounded finish and no bitterness; the finer modern lots are cleaner and show a little dried fruit. Simmered, it makes the thick red-brown liquor that takes butter or milk; brewed gongfu after two rinses it gives seven or eight steeps. The small cubes are built for a thermos and are the easiest way to drink it at a desk.

It is sold by pressing year and factory – the Ya'an and Yingjing tea factories are the historic makers – in formats from the 500 g border brick to gift tins; price rises with the leaf grade and the packaging rather than with age. Look for a sweet, woody, clean smell and a firm, dry brick; the marketing ('thirty-two steps', health claims) can be ignored in favour of the cup.

If you want the authentic version, buy a plain Kang Zhuan; if you want the easy version, buy the cubes and keep a few in your bag for winter.
sources_note: 'Ya'an Zang Cha' geographical indication is dated to 2008 in Chinese sources; stated as 'the 2000s'. The 'thirty-two steps' figure is a marketing claim used by Ya'an makers and is mentioned only as such.
